The first of the six optimal edit paths, each costing 1, maps A to X, B to Y and C to Z (matching colors in both graphs and the card); the path's two edges land on X–Y and Y–Z, and the triangle's third edge Z–X, dashed in accent, is the one insertion." width="100%"} An edit path is a complete account of how this graph turns into a graph isomorphic to `other=`: every node of this graph is substituted by a node of `other=` or deleted, every node of `other=` not substituted is inserted, and the same holds for edges. The cost of the cheapest path is the exact graph edit distance, the value returned by `graph_edit_distance(exact=True)`; this method also returns the paths themselves, all of them when several reach the minimum. For isomorphic graphs the cost is `0` and the paths are the isomorphisms between the two graphs. Edit paths are useful to: - explain a graph edit distance, by showing which nodes and edges correspond - align two small networks (molecules, workflows, circuits) node by node - enumerate the different ways two structures can be matched at the same cost The search is exponential in the worst case and is practical for graphs of up to about a dozen nodes. Labels play no part, and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The target graph. It must have the same directedness as the calling graph. An edge's dictionary holds its attributes plus its `"weight"` when it has one. See `graph_edit_distance()`. If no edit path costs this much or less, the result is `([], None)`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A pair `(paths, cost)`. Each path is a tuple `(node_path, edge_path)`: `node_path` lists `(u, v)` pairs of node IDs of this graph and of `other=`, and `edge_path` lists `(e, f)` pairs of edge IDs. A `None` on the left is an insertion and a `None` on the right a deletion. `cost` is the minimum cost, a `float`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs differ in directedness, or a cost is negative or not a number. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~graph_edit_distance`) : The edit distance alone, label-based or exact. [](`~optimize_edit_paths`) : Iterate over edit paths of decreasing cost. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Uses the branch-and-bound search described in `graph_edit_distance()`, keeping every complete path whose cost ties the best one found. Every cheapest node correspondence is listed; for each, the edges are matched by one optimal assignment. Unlike NetworkX's `optimal_edit_paths()`, the edge path pairs edge IDs rather than `(u, v)` endpoint tuples, so that parallel edges stay distinguishable. The order of the paths can differ from NetworkX's, since equally good assignments may be explored in a different order. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A three-node path becomes a triangle by inserting one edge. The path can be laid onto the triangle in six ways (any of the three nodes can take the middle position, in either orientation), so there are six optimal edit paths: ::: {#683a2e23 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]).add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) triangle = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]) triangle.add_edges([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z"), ("Z", "X")]) paths, cost = path.optimal_edit_paths(triangle) len(paths), cost ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6, 1.0) ``` ::: ::: Each path pairs node IDs and edge IDs. In the first path, the one inserted edge shows up as an edge pair with `None` on the left: ::: {#6387e0e7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} node_path, edge_path = paths[0] node_path, edge_path ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)], [(1, 1), (2, 2), (None, 3)]) ``` ::: :::
